title: Portulan Pack Definition v1.0
description: The manifest at the root of a pack. A pack is the cascade's middle layer — core < pack < workspace < repo card < task — and this manifest declares what it contributes to that cascade: skills, personas, verify recipes, and gate-policy fragments. It is an index, not a container, for the same reason the Workspace Definition is: the content lives in the files the paths point at. Written in the same deliberately small subset of JSON Schema 2020-12 — see spec/README.md for the subset, for what validates this, and for why a pack carries its own version train rather than the Workspace Definition's.

portulan.description: Version block. `pack` is the Pack Definition version this manifest is written against. It is deliberately NOT the Workspace Definition version: a pack and a workspace are different artifacts validated against different contracts, and one number governing both would make a bump in either mean a change in the other. `doctor` refuses a manifest naming a version ahead of the one it implements rather than grading it against a contract it was not written for.

pack.description: Pack Definition version, MAJOR.MINOR. A MAJOR bump means a migration exists.

version.description: Optional version of this pack's own content, SemVer. Distinct from `pack` above, which versions the contract. A pack shipped through a feed is pinned by consumers on this, and it moves independently of the engine. THIS FIELD IS HOW INDEPENDENT VERSIONING IS EXPRESSED, and a git tag is not — re-derived by measurement on CLI 2.1.220, 2026-07-29, because an earlier note in .portulan/handoffs/2026-07-26-the-tag-and-the-install.md reached the opposite guess and said its own basis had gone stale. What was measured: an installed marketplace is not a git working clone at all (no `.git`; contents carry a `.gcs-sha` marker), and an install is cached at `<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version>/` with several versions of one plugin coexisting, resolved from the manifest's version field. Tags cannot participate in that path. Re-measure on CLI upgrade — this is a fact about one version.

name.description: Stable identifier for this pack, unique within its category. The canonical reference a workspace's `packs` array carries is `category/name` — this manifest owns that form, and resolution maps it to an installed pack. The workspace schema deliberately keeps `packs` items as free strings: tightening them to this shape would be a constraint a manifest could newly fail, which is a MAJOR bump on the other train.

category.description: Which of the three pack kinds this is, spelled as the directory that holds it so the canonical `category/name` reference and the tree agree by construction. The distinction is not decorative: a stack pack profiles a language or framework, a tool pack integrates a tool or MCP server and ships the gate classification for each, and a ritual pack carries a repeatable procedure that composes onto the loop.

summary.description: One line an agent can read before loading anything else.

doc.description: Where this pack's content, rationale and honest limits are written up. The `why` half, kept in Markdown, in the same split the Workspace Definition uses for `gates` and `slots.gates`: this manifest is the machine-readable index, and the prose it points at is what a human reads.

contributes.description: What this pack adds to the cascade. Every key is optional and an absent key contributes nothing of that kind — but the object itself is required, because a pack contributing nothing is a plugin, not a pack, and the manifest should say which it is rather than leaving it to be inferred from four absences.

skills.description: Skill roots this pack ships, each a directory that either IS one skill (holding SKILL.md) or CONTAINS them. The bound a walk of these roots MUST observe — descend to a fixed depth and report where it stopped, rather than reporting green over what it did not look at — is the SHAPE fixed by .portulan/tasks/0008-a-declared-skills-path-sees-one-level-down.md. That task set the number for `plugin-lint`, which walks a PLUGIN's declared skills path; `doctor` walks THIS key as of 2026-08-03 and takes the same number deliberately, so two walkers over one declared key cannot disagree about how deep a skill may sit. The first cut of doctor's walk took a different number AND returned silently at the limit, which made a skill below the bound invisible — the exact green-over-what-it-did-not-look-at this sentence forbids, shipped inside the change that quotes it. OPENED AS OF 2026-08-03, and this note has now been wrong in both directions, which is why it records the correction rather than being rewritten clean. `doctor` walks these roots and validates each `SKILL.md`'s frontmatter, to the depth .portulan/tasks/0008 fixes, reporting where it stopped. It previously said `doctor` counted the paths into its pack report line and opened none of them — true when written. Composition into a host is a different question and is still row 7's clause (b). MILESTONE 7 COMMITTED THE CONSUMER, and this is the clause that changed: row 7 of docs/plan.md carries the amendment of 2026-07-30 (argument in docs/milestones/m07.md), whose clause (b) requires that a composed pack's skills be INVOCABLE through a host — a checkpoint skill from a composed pack invoked in the adopting workspace the same way a core skill is, with that parity as the demonstration. Reaching parity means reading this key, so the row has undertaken to open it. The clause here said the opposite until 2026-07-31, and it was not wrong when written: it was authored on one branch while clause (b) was merging on another, and it went stale nine minutes after it landed — a rule with two carriers, drifting at the weaker one, arriving by concurrency rather than by neglect. Named at all because a contribution kind that is counted but never opened is the one a reader most easily assumes is wired.

personas.description: Persona files this pack ships, each carrying the five-part contract core/personas/README.md fixes: a `tools:` allow-list, a charter, autonomy reach in tier vocabulary, a memory scope, and a read/write posture. The memory scope is the persona's own field and is deliberately not duplicated here — a pack distributes per-persona material its adopter does not own. READ BY TWO CONSUMERS: cli/index.mjs resolves and opens this key as of Workspace Definition 2.6, deriving each persona's declared scope into the adopting workspace's own layer; and as of 2026-08-03 `doctor` opens it too, grading each persona against the five-part contract core/personas/README.md fixes — including the memory scope this field's own description names, which is the half core/operating/memory.md promised would be validated at milestone 7. Both carry the containment check that goes with opening a path — see `$defs/filePath`. **Corrected at the milestone-6 close:** this note said where that material's scope is declared was a question core/operating/memory.md HOLDS OPEN. That file now settles it — the first instance is declared at milestone 6 and validated at milestone 7 — so the clause described the tree as it was before the page it cites was written.

verify.description: Verify recipes this pack offers. DECLARED, not merged, as of Workspace Definition 2.7: nothing today folds these into a workspace's recipe set, and a workspace runs the recipes its own manifest declares. Said here rather than left to be discovered, because a recipe that looks composed and is not would be a green covering something nobody ran. MILESTONE 7 COMMITS A COMPOSING CONSUMER, on the maintainer's ruling of 2026-07-31 and under a contract stated in row 7 of docs/plan.md rather than left to the implementation: composition is ADDITIVE ONLY — a pack may add a recipe and may never redefine, remove or replace one the workspace declares, nor become the workspace's `verify.default` — and a composed recipe is namespaced by its pack, so a collision is impossible rather than resolved. The limits are not a security boundary and should not be read as one: a recipe's `run` is arbitrary shell, and a workspace that lists a pack has already consented to running that pack's code. What they prevent is narrower and is the thing worth preventing — a pack silently changing what this workspace's green MEANS, by shadowing a recipe the workspace owns or by becoming the recipe the Stop-gate runs on its own. IT LANDED at milestone 7 session 6: `cli/recipe-set.mjs` is the composing consumer and the one carrier of the runnable set, and CI calls it rather than enumerating a manifest — so the declare-only state above is now history rather than description, and is kept as history because this note has been wrong in both directions and records its corrections instead of being rewritten clean. What a reader needs now: a composed recipe's id becomes `<category>/<name>:<id>`, applied by the carrier and never taken from the pack's own spelling, which is what makes a collision with a workspace id impossible rather than resolved — a workspace id and `verify.default` are both `$defs/slug`, and `/` and `:` are outside that grammar.

gates.description: Gate-policy fragments — the cascade's missing middle, and the contribution that needs care, because an installed pack reaching the gate map means a dependency can change what an agent is allowed to do. The floor is the maintainer's ruling of 2026-07-27 recorded in .portulan/proposals/0010-prohibited-as-a-fourth-universal-tier.md: a pack may raise a tier or add a prohibition, and may NEVER demote another layer's classification. Enforcement is split between this schema and the merge step, and the split is stated rather than implied — see `$defs/fragment`. READ TODAY, like `personas` and unlike `skills` and `verify`: cli/compile.mjs is the merge step, and it resolves this key when a pack root is given.

slug.description: A lowercase hyphenated identifier. Defined once and referenced everywhere an id is used or named, so the constraint cannot drift between the field that declares an id and the field that points at one.

filePath.description: A relative path to a file inside this pack, resolved from the PACK root. The leading character may not be `/` (no absolute paths), `:` is excluded (no URLs), and `.` is excluded so that neither `./` nor `../` can BEGIN a value — which is where this differs from the Workspace Definition's equivalent, and it is deliberate: a workspace may legitimately point at a constitution that lives beside it, but a pack reaching outside its own directory is reaching into the adopter's tree, which is the one direction the cascade does not run. WHAT THIS PATTERN DOES NOT DO, measured rather than assumed: it bars only the LEADING form. `a/../../x` matches it and still escapes. Containment is not a pattern's job — the same conclusion `actionPath` reaches from the other side, and the one cli/compile.mjs already acts on by resolving its policy path and checking containment AFTER resolution. **Corrected at the milestone-6 close, which found this note describing an earlier state of the tree.** It said nothing resolved these paths and that an escaping value was therefore inert. Since Workspace Definition 2.6 `cli/index.mjs` **does** resolve and open `contributes.personas`, and it already carries the containment check the sentence assigned to milestone 7 — `fs.realpathSync` on both the pack directory and the file, compared AFTER resolution, refusing a persona that lands outside the pack. So the pattern is not the only guard, and never was the one that mattered. **Corrected again 2026-08-03, when the remaining half arrived.** The sentence above said `doctor` validates shape and does not open what a manifest points at, and that `contributes.skills` is opened by nothing so an escaping value there is still inert. Both halves are now false: `doctor` opens the skills roots and the persona files, and an escaping value is therefore no longer inert — so the containment check landed in the same change as the opening, resolved-then-compared exactly as cli/index.mjs does, rather than being left to this pattern. That is the general lesson this field keeps teaching: a value is inert only while nothing reads it, and 'nothing reads it' is a fact with an expiry date. Must not end in `/`.

dirPath.description: A relative path to a directory inside this pack — the same rules as `filePath`, INCLUDING its stated limit: the leading `../` form is barred and a `..` segment deeper in the value is not, so containment belongs to the consumer that resolves these paths rather than to this pattern. Must end in `/`, so the intent is legible without touching the filesystem.

recipe.description: One verify recipe: what to run, and what it needs in order to run at all. The same shape the Workspace Definition uses, repeated rather than shared because the two schemas are on separate version trains and a shared definition would couple their bumps — which is the coupling this split exists to avoid.

run.description: The command, as it would be typed from the ADOPTING repository's root — which is a root this pack cannot know. A pack names its own files with `${PACK_ROOT}`, expanded by the composing consumer (`cli/recipe-set.mjs`) to the pack's resolved root relative to that repository root, before the command reaches a shell: `bash ${PACK_ROOT}/verify/thing.sh`. After expansion the first sentence is true again, which is the point. Expansion runs BEFORE the newline-and-tab refusal, so a pack root carrying one cannot pass a check that ran too early. A WORKSPACE recipe's `run` is never expanded — the token has no meaning outside a pack, and rewriting it there would be a consumer inventing a feature the Workspace Definition does not declare.

requires.description: The tools the recipe needs. Declared rather than discovered, because a recipe that cannot run must be distinguishable from one that ran and failed — the difference between exit 2 and exit 1.

doc.description: Where the recipe's checks and their known limits are written up. Resolved from the PACK root, like every other path in this manifest — unlike the sibling `run`, which is a command line and is therefore written as it would be typed from the repository root.

fragment.description: One gate-policy fragment: an id-addressed rule this pack contributes, in the same shape .portulan/gates.json already uses, because that policy was deliberately modelled as a list of id-addressed rules with no dependence on being the only source so that a merge step would be an addition rather than a redesign (.portulan/compile/README.md). WHERE THE TIGHTEN-ONLY RULE IS ENFORCED, stated plainly because a schema implying a guarantee it does not carry is what .portulan/dod.md condition 4 refuses: tightening is relative to what the same id already holds in the layer beneath, and a manifest cannot see that layer. So the shape forecloses what shape can — `auto` is not in the tier enum below, which makes demotion-to-unattended unexpressible in a pack at all — and the remaining comparisons are the merge step's. TIGHTENING HAS TWO AXES AND THE MERGE CHECKS BOTH. The tier may only rise. The `action` may not change at all: a fragment naming an existing id must carry that rule's action unaltered, because raising the tier while replacing the matcher passes every tier comparison, is reported as a tightening, and removes the gate — measured, on a real policy, as a fragment that took `git push --force` from gated to prohibited and deleted the emitted gate in the same move. A pack that wants to gate a different action contributes a NEW id; changing what an existing rule matches belongs to the workspace, which owns its policy. Neither layer is sufficient alone, and a release that consumes fragments without the merge's refusals would be trusting what it claims to check.

id.description: The rule this fragment declares or tightens. A fragment naming an id no lower layer carries is a pure addition; one naming an existing id is a tightening, and is refused at the merge unless its tier is stronger AND its action is identical. Ids are greppable by design and ship in core, so knowing one is not a barrier — which is exactly why the action must be preserved rather than trusted.

tier.description: The tier this fragment asserts. THREE values where core names four: `auto` is deliberately absent. A pack may only ever add restriction, and `auto` is the absence of restriction — it compiles to nothing (the compiler emits `ask` and `deny`, never `allow`), so a pack declaring it could only be attempting to demote an id a lower layer restricts. Barring it here is the one part of the rule a manifest's shape can enforce on its own, and it costs a pack nothing it should want: a pack with no opinion about an action simply omits the fragment.

action.description: What the rule matches, in the workspace's own action vocabulary rather than any host's — the same four kinds .portulan/gates.json uses. `none` is the honest one: an action with no tool-level surface, named so the gap is visible instead of implied by a sentence covering more than its matcher does. Exactly one kind per fragment: the branches below each close themselves, which is what makes `{"write": …, "shell": …}` fail rather than silently matching on whichever the compiler happened to read first.

oneOf.description: A path this rule protects from writes.
A path this rule governs reads of.
A command prefix, matched as a shell command rather than as a tool name.
No tool-level surface. The value is the explanation of why, which is the whole point of the kind: a matcher pretending to cover this would be worse than the honest gap.

reason.description: Why the rule exists, in the pack author's own words, and what the agent should do instead. Required rather than optional because a rule with no rationale is taste, and because this sentence is what an adopter reads when a pack they installed refuses something — a refusal whose reason is a pack name is indistinguishable from a bug.

actionPath.description: A path a gate rule matches, resolved from the ADOPTER's repository root rather than from the pack — a pack gating its own directory would be gating files nobody edits. No absolute paths and no URLs. UNLIKE the pack-internal `filePath` and `dirPath`, a leading `.` is permitted and must be, because the action vocabulary's real values include `./` and `.portulan/`; that also means this pattern does NOT exclude `../`, and saying so is the point. Containment is not a pattern's job — a `../` chain passes any regex and still escapes, which is why cli/compile.mjs resolves its policy path and checks containment AFTER resolution rather than by pattern alone. What bounds the damage here is the direction of the whole mechanism: a fragment can only ever ADD restriction, and the compiler emits `ask` and `deny` and never `allow`, so a fragment naming a path outside the adopter's tree gates something nobody touches. That is noise, not a breach — and it is stated rather than papered over with a pattern that would look like a containment check while being none.
